posts.title: 2026.46: The End of Jensen
posts.summary: The best Stratechery content from the week of November 9, 2026, including the shocking demise of Jensen Huang; enterprise, consumer and Intel; and professional basketbal.
bullets: Jensen Huang has concluded his 32-year tenure as CEO of Nvidia, marking a massive leadership transition for the most critical company in the AI hardware ecosystem.
Intel continues to struggle with its foundry strategy and AI-era competitiveness, contrasting sharply with AMD’s success in capturing enterprise demand.
The divergence between Intel and AMD is attributed to fundamental differences in chiplet architecture, corporate culture, and long-term strategic execution.
The sudden departure of Huang raises significant questions regarding Nvidia's future trajectory and the broader implications for American technological dominance.

posts.title: CATL targets 6,000 passenger car battery swap stations in 2027, potentially overtaking Nio
posts.summary:
CATL's plan includes 5,000 urban stations and 1,000 highway stations, covering 297 cities in China.
For details, please visit CnEVPost (cnev.co).
bullets: CATL aims to operate 6,000 passenger car battery swap stations by 2027, covering 297 cities and positioning itself to potentially overtake Nio as China's largest swap network operator.
The expansion plan includes 5,000 urban stations to ensure 10-minute accessibility in core areas and 1,000 highway stations across 20 major transit routes.
CATL's aggressive growth is supported by strategic partnerships, including a recent deal with BAIC Group to integrate multiple brands into the Choco swap ecosystem.

Nio currently operates 4,254 stations, and while it continues to add roughly 1,000 units annually, CATL's rapid deployment pace threatens to shift the competitive landscape of battery-as-a-service infrastructure.

posts.title: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
posts.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong? —Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square The self-styled visionaries…
bullets: Nvidia has privately confirmed to lawmakers that geotracking advanced AI chips is technically feasible, contradicting public claims by industry groups that such measures are infeasible.
The proposed Chip Security Act aims to implement these tracking requirements to prevent the smuggling of high-end AI hardware to China.
The industry faces significant political instability following a major Microsoft service outage and a strategic miscalculation by tech leaders regarding the recent midterm election outcomes.
Nvidia is navigating internal leadership transitions following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang amid personal controversy.

posts.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
posts.summary:
300mm SiC breakthrough; Nvidia faces questions about security and oversight; Siemens buys Lauterbach; chiplet standards; new memory bets; imec interposer process flow; TPUs with CPUs; 2D transistors; anti-smuggling tools for chips.
The post Chip Industry Week In Review appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Infineon achieved a major manufacturing milestone by producing 300mm silicon carbide (SiC) power devices, which can yield 2.3 times more chips per wafer than 200mm alternatives.
Google expanded its AI hardware portfolio with the 8th-gen TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx, the latter of which utilizes AMD EPYC CPUs to enhance secure and confidential inference capabilities.
AMD launched its 6th-gen EPYC processors, featuring a new AI GPU equipped with 288GB of HBM4 memory, signaling a significant step forward in high-density compute offerings.
Nvidia faces mounting regulatory and legal scrutiny following reports that its leadership was aware of chip-smuggling investigations involving the 'Megaspeed' entity prior to the current scandal.
Imec has finalized baseline process flows for its NanoIC silicon-interposer platform, with a PDK release scheduled for early 2027 to support advanced chiplet and 3D integration.

posts.title: Shifting HBM4 Controller Functions Closer To Memory (UC Riverside)
posts.summary:
Tharunya Yogananda and Wantong Li of the University of California, Riverside published a technical paper titled “Beyond Host-Side Control: HBM Controller Partitioning Across Host and HBM Base Dies.” Abstract Excerpt: “Recent generations of high bandwidth memory (HBM), such as HBM4, allow the base die of the memory stack to be manufactured using a logic process... » read more
The post Shifting HBM4 Controller Functions Closer To Memory (UC Riverside) appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering.
bullets: Researchers at UC Riverside have conducted the first systematic study on partitioning HBM4 controller functions between the host processor and the memory base die.
The study evaluates four distinct placement strategies, ranging from host-only control to full base-die integration, to optimize performance and maintenance.
Leveraging the logic-capable base die of HBM4 allows for more complex scheduling and maintenance tasks to be offloaded from the host, potentially reducing latency and improving bandwidth efficiency.
This research provides a critical architectural framework for future high-performance computing systems that rely on tighter integration between memory and logic.
